\chapter{El taller}
\label{ch:es-taller}
\hlchaptermodality{449}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can leave a bike at a repair shop and understand the slip that comes back: say which part has failed, ask whether it can be fixed by a given day, and ask somebody to pass me a tool.}

Read the message or notice this chapter's words exist for, then say the same thing back.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[arreglar]{arreglar — putting it right}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-arreglar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{reparar} and \textbf{estropeado}. One undoes the other.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: arreglar}
\textbf{arreglar} — to fix, to mend, to sort out.

\emph{¿Me puedes arreglar la bici?} — can you fix my bike for me? \emph{Han arreglado el ascensor} — they've fixed the lift. \emph{Ya está arreglado} — it's sorted now.

And beyond machinery: \emph{arreglar los papeles} — sort the paperwork out. \emph{Arreglar una habitación} — tidy a room. \emph{Arreglarse} — get yourself ready to go out.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: arreglar and reparar}]
Both mean to fix, and a Spanish speaker reaches for them differently:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{word} & \textbf{where it sits} \\
\midrule
\textbf{arreglar} & everyday speech, and things that are not machines \\
\textbf{reparar} & the workshop, the invoice, the written notice \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\emph{He arreglado la silla} is what you tell a friend. \emph{Reparación de calzado} is what the shop window says. You can \emph{arreglar} an argument or a haircut; \emph{reparar} neither.

Where the object is a broken machine, the two overlap and either is correct. Take \textbf{arreglar} as your default and you will be right far more often.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Break it as \textbf{a-rregl-ar}, and the middle is \textbf{regla} — a ruler, a rule — from Latin \textbf{regula}, the carpenter's straight edge.

So to \emph{arreglar} something is to bring it back to the straight edge: the plank is warped, you true it. You met the same \emph{regula} in \textbf{regular}. English took it too, in \emph{regulate}, \emph{rule} and \emph{ruler}, and kept the tool and the law in one word as Spanish does.

The \textbf{rr} is where the \emph{a-} meets the \emph{r-} of \emph{regla}. Spanish doubles it and rolls it, and the doubling is the only trace left of the prefix.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item can you fix my bike?
  \item it's sorted now
  \item which of the two verbs belongs on a shop sign
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
To fix? (\textbf{Arreglar}.) What tool is hiding inside it? (\textbf{La regla}, the straight edge.) What does \emph{arreglarse} mean about a person? (\textbf{Getting ready to go out}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el freno]{el freno — what stops you}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-freno}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la bicicleta} and \textbf{arreglar}. Name the part most often needing the second.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el freno}
\textbf{el freno} — the brake.

\emph{Los frenos no van} — the brakes aren't working. \emph{El freno de mano} — the handbrake. \emph{Frenar} — to brake: \emph{frena antes de la curva}, brake before the bend.

Spanish uses the plural far more than English does. A bicycle has \emph{frenos}, and asking about \emph{el freno} on a bike would sound as though you knew which one was at fault.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the noun and the verb in one step}]
\textbf{el freno} gives \textbf{frenar} by adding nothing but \emph{-ar}, and this pair is one instance of a pattern you can lean on:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{noun} & \textbf{verb from it} \\
\midrule
el freno & fren\textbf{ar} — to brake \\
la planta & plant\textbf{ar} — to plant \\
el arreglo & arregl\textbf{ar} — to fix \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Note the third row runs backwards from the other two: \textbf{el arreglo} is the noun built from the verb, not the verb built from the noun. Spanish makes these in both directions and the ending alone will not tell you which came first — a question for a dictionary, not for a rule.

What you can rely on is the shape: meeting a noun, try \emph{-ar} on it; meeting an \emph{-ar} verb, try cutting it back to a noun. You will be right often enough to make it worth the guess.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{frenum}, the bit — the metal bar in a horse's mouth that the reins pull on. That is the oldest brake there is, and the word moved onto carts, then bicycles, then cars, without ever changing its job.

English has the same word in the medical \textbf{frenulum}, the small fold of tissue under your tongue, so called because it holds the tongue back. Spanish keeps the sense alive too: \emph{poner freno a algo} — to put a stop to something.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the brakes aren't working
  \item can you fix the brakes?
  \item the verb that goes with \emph{el freno}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The brake? (\textbf{El freno}.) On a bike, singular or plural? (\textbf{Plural} — \emph{los frenos}.) What was a \emph{frenum} originally? (\textbf{The bit in a horse's mouth}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la rueda]{la rueda — the wheel}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-rueda}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{alrededor} and \textbf{la bicicleta}. There is a wheel inside one of those words, and it is not the obvious one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la rueda}
\textbf{la rueda} — the wheel, and on a car the tyre as well.

\emph{La rueda de atrás} — the back wheel. \emph{Se me ha pinchado una rueda} — I've got a puncture. \emph{La rueda de repuesto} — the spare.

A bicycle has \emph{dos ruedas}, and Spanish will name a vehicle by counting them: \emph{un vehículo de dos ruedas}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the o that breaks in two}]
Latin \emph{rota} has an \textbf{o}. Spanish has \textbf{ue}. That change is everywhere once you look for it, and it happens under one condition — stress:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{unstressed o} & \textbf{stressed, so ue} \\
\midrule
r\textbf{o}dar — to roll & la r\textbf{ue}da \\
p\textbf{o}der — to be able & p\textbf{ue}do \\
v\textbf{o}lver — to return & v\textbf{ue}lvo \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \emph{rueda} and \emph{rodar} one after the other and you can hear the same word twice. The vowel splits under the weight of the stress and closes up again when the stress moves off.

This is why so many Spanish verbs look irregular and are not. They are one vowel obeying one condition.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{rota}, wheel. And here is the payoff on a word you already use daily.

\textbf{Alrededor} is \emph{al} + \emph{rededor}, and \emph{rededor} comes from Latin \textbf{retrō}, \emph{backwards} — \textbf{pulled sideways by \emph{rota}}, the wheel. That is the careful version and it is worth keeping careful: \emph{rota} is not where the word started, it is what bent it on the way. Both ideas ended up inside it, which is why something \emph{alrededor} is behind you as well as in front.

The wheel half is generous. A \textbf{rotunda} is a round building, a \textbf{rotation} turns, Spanish keeps \emph{rotonda} for the roundabout you drive round, and \emph{la rodilla} — the knee — is \emph{rotella}, a little wheel. A knee and the space around you, named by the same rolling.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the back wheel and the spare wheel
  \item the brakes and the wheel need fixing
  \item what \emph{alrededor} has to do with \emph{rueda}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The wheel? (\textbf{La rueda}.) Why \emph{ue} and not \emph{o}? (\textbf{The stress falls on it}.) What is the unstressed verb alongside it? (\textbf{Rodar}, to roll.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el taladro]{el taladro — the drill}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-taladro}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{la mano} and \textbf{la madera}. One holds the tool, the other takes the hole.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: el taladro}
\textbf{el taladro} — the drill.

\emph{¿Me dejas el taladro?} — can you lend me the drill? \emph{Taladrar} — to drill: \emph{hay que taladrar la pared}, we need to drill the wall.

The word covers the machine and, in a workshop, the bit as well. \emph{Un taladro para madera} is a wood bit; \emph{un taladro sin cable} is a cordless drill.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: lending, in Spanish}]
Asking to borrow a tool is where two verbs get tangled, because Spanish has no verb for \emph{borrow} at all:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{what you want} & \textbf{what Spanish says} \\
\midrule
lend me the drill & \emph{¿me \textbf{dejas} el taladro?} \\
can I borrow it? & \emph{¿me lo \textbf{prestas}?} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both put the \textbf{lender} in the subject position. There is no sentence shaped like \emph{I borrow the drill from you}; you turn it round and ask the other person to do the lending. \emph{Dejar} is the everyday one and \emph{prestar} the slightly more formal.

Hand the tool back with \emph{aquí tienes} and you have the whole exchange.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Latin \textbf{taratrum}, a borer — itself taken from Gaulish, the Celtic language spoken in France before Latin arrived. The Romans met a better tool than their own and kept the name with it.

From \emph{taratrum} to \emph{taladro} an \textbf{r} turned into an \textbf{l}, and notice that \emph{taratrum} has no \emph{l} to begin with. The word had \textbf{two r's}, which is awkward, so one of them gave way — a repeated sound in one short word is unstable, and changing one of the pair is the easiest repair.

That is not what happened to \emph{milagro} and \emph{peligro}. Those came from \emph{miraculum} and \emph{periculum}, which \textbf{did} have both letters, and the two traded places. Two different habits, worth telling apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item can you lend me the drill?
  \item we have to drill the wall
  \item why \emph{milagro} and \emph{taladro} are the same kind of case
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
The drill? (\textbf{El taladro}.) To drill? (\textbf{Taladrar}.) How do you ask to borrow something? (\textbf{By asking the other person to lend it} — \emph{¿me dejas…?})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[acercar]{acercar — pass it here}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-acercar}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{cerca} and \textbf{acercarse}. Now take the \emph{-se} off the second one and see what is left.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: acercar}
\textbf{acercar} — to bring something closer, and so, constantly, \textbf{to pass}.

\emph{¿Me acercas el taladro?} — can you pass me the drill? \emph{Acerca la silla} — pull your chair up. \emph{Te acerco a la estación} — I'll run you to the station.

That last one is worth keeping. Offering somebody a lift in Spanish is offering to \emph{acercar} them: you are bringing them nearer to where they are going.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one verb, two directions}]
You already own the \emph{-se} version. Here they are side by side:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{form} & \textbf{who moves} \\
\midrule
\textbf{acercarse} & the subject — \emph{me acerco a la puerta} \\
\textbf{acercar} & something else — \emph{acerco la silla} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Without the \emph{-se}, the verb needs an object; the thing that comes closer is whatever you name. With the \emph{-se}, the subject is the thing that comes closer. That is the same switch you saw in \emph{mudar} and \emph{mudarse}, and it runs through hundreds of Spanish verbs.

So in a workshop, \emph{acércate} means come over here, and \emph{acércamelo} means send it over here. One syllable apart, and two different people doing the moving.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{a-cerc-ar}: the prefix \emph{a-} meaning towards, the \emph{cerca} you already say, and the \emph{-ar} of an ordinary verb. The middle is Latin \textbf{circa}, around, and its ring is still visible in \emph{círculo} and in English \emph{circle} and \emph{circa}.

The road from \textquotedblleft{}around\textquotedblright{} to \textquotedblleft{}near\textquotedblright{} is short: things arranged around you are the things close to you. Spanish turned the circle into a distance, then built a verb on it, and the verb now does the job of the English \emph{pass}, \emph{pull up} and \emph{give a lift} all at once.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item can you pass me the drill?
  \item pull your chair up
  \item I'll run you to the station
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Pass me the drill? (\textbf{¿Me acercas el taladro?}) Who moves with \emph{acercarse}? (\textbf{The subject}.) What does \emph{te acerco a la estación} offer? (\textbf{A lift}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[(arreglar, el freno, la rueda, el …]{(arreglar, el freno, la rueda, el taladro, acercar) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ES-R449-repaso-taller}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say all five: \emph{to fix}, \emph{the brake}, \emph{the wheel}, \emph{the drill}, \emph{to pass}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: each noun brought a verb with it}]
Three of these five came in pairs, and the second half of each pair cost you nothing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{the noun} & \textbf{its verb} \\
\midrule
el freno & \textbf{frenar} — to brake \\
la rueda & \textbf{rodar} — to roll \\
el taladro & \textbf{taladrar} — to drill \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Note that \emph{rodar} does not keep the \emph{ue}. The \textbf{ue} appears only where the stress lands on it, so the noun has it and the infinitive does not. If you try to say \emph{ruedar} you will be corrected; if you say \emph{rueda} and \emph{rodamos} you will not.

That one condition — stress — accounts for most of what looks irregular in Spanish verbs, and you now have a noun that shows it standing still.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the -se you keep meeting}]
Three verbs in two chapters have turned on the same small word:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{without -se} & \textbf{with -se} \\
\midrule
\emph{mudar} — change a thing & \emph{mudarse} — move house \\
\emph{acercar} — bring it closer & \emph{acercarse} — come closer \\
\emph{arreglar} — fix a thing & \emph{arreglarse} — get ready \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Read the right-hand column and one thing is constant: the subject is on the receiving end. Read the left and the verb is reaching out to an object. When you meet a new verb in both shapes, that question sorts them before you look anything up.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the brakes aren't working and the back wheel is loose
  \item can you fix it today?
  \item the verbs belonging to \emph{freno}, \emph{rueda} and \emph{taladro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
All five again, in Spanish, without looking. Then one sentence that puts a tool in somebody's hand.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{(dejar la bici en el taller) — read it, then do it yourself}

\label{lesson:ES-C449-sintesis-taller}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{arreglar} and \textbf{el freno}. Both are on the slip below.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
The slip handed back across the counter. Read it, then answer.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Taller de bicicletas — resguardo}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Bicicleta azul, sin cesta. Entra el martes.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Los \textbf{frenos} de atrás no van. Se cambian.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
La \textbf{rueda} delantera está bien; solo hay que apretarla.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
Presupuesto: 24 €. Se \textbf{arregla} para el jueves.
\end{quote}

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item which part is being replaced and which is only being tightened
  \item what it will cost and when it will be ready
  \item what day the bike went in
\end{itemize}

\begin{culture}
Look at \textbf{se cambian} and \textbf{se arregla}. Neither says who does the work, and on a repair slip that is the point: the shop is not the subject of a sentence, the job is. Spanish gets there with \emph{se} plus the verb, and the verb agrees with the thing being done — \emph{frenos} is plural so \emph{cambian} is plural, \emph{la bicicleta} is singular so \emph{arregla} is singular.

English reaches for the passive here: \emph{the brakes are being changed}. Spanish reaches for \emph{se}. Once you notice it you will see it on every notice and every menu: \emph{se alquila}, \emph{se vende}, \emph{se ruega}.

And \textbf{solo hay que apretarla} does the same job a third way — no subject at all, only a thing that must be done.
\end{culture}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Now your turn, out loud and then in writing. Four lines handing a bike over: say what is wrong with the brakes, say the front wheel is fine, ask whether they can fix it by Friday, and ask them to pass you the drill so you can do one part yourself.

Then check yourself: did you use \emph{se} for the work being done, and did the verb agree with the part rather than with the shop?
\end{tcolorbox}
